lesson.title: Filling the Balloon: Relating Volume and Radius Over Time
lesson.summary: Pumping air into a balloon at a constant volume rate does not make the radius grow at a constant rate, because the same extra volume has to stretch over more and more surface as the balloon gets bigger, and the sphere volume formula shows exactly why.
lesson.body:
A spherical balloon being inflated is a natural setting for related rates because the relevant geometric fact, the volume formula for a sphere, is something you already know, and the related rates diagram is just a circle labeled with radius r. As with every classic problem, the goal is to connect a known rate, here the rate air is pumped in, to an unknown rate, how fast the radius is growing, at one specific instant.

The volume of a sphere is V = (4/3) pi r^3. Since both V and r are changing over time as the balloon inflates, differentiate this equation with respect to t: dV/dt = 4 pi r^2 (dr/dt), using the power rule on r^3 together with the chain rule, since r itself depends on t.

Here is the fully worked example. Air is pumped into a spherical balloon at a rate of 100 cubic centimeters per second. Find the rate the radius is increasing at the moment the radius is 5 centimeters. Substitute dV/dt = 100 and r = 5 into dV/dt = 4 pi r^2 (dr/dt): 100 = 4 pi (25)(dr/dt) = 100 pi (dr/dt). Solving for the unknown rate: dr/dt = 100 / (100 pi) = 1/pi centimeters per second, which is approximately 0.318 centimeters per second.

It is worth pausing on why this rate is not simply constant, even though the pump is putting in air at a perfectly constant 100 cubic centimeters per second. The equation dV/dt = 4 pi r^2 (dr/dt) shows that the same fixed dV/dt has to be divided by 4 pi r^2 to get dr/dt, and that r^2 term grows as the balloon expands. In other words, the same volume of new air has to spread over a larger and larger surface, 4 pi r^2 being exactly the surface area of the sphere, so it stretches the radius by a smaller and smaller amount as the balloon gets bigger. A balloon that is already large grows in radius much more slowly than a small one, for the same pumping rate, which matches the everyday experience that a balloon feels easiest to inflate near the very start.

In the language of rate variables, dV/dt = 100 is the given rate, positive because the balloon is inflating, dr/dt is the unknown rate, also positive since the radius is growing, and r = 5 is an instantaneous value describing the one moment in question, not a rate at all, which is exactly the kind of sorting that step one of the related rates setup method asks you to do before writing any equation.
